opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot in the context of AI safety specifically. Right now, if you look at technical safety research, a big bottleneck isn't really money. It's that there just aren't that many people who can take a grant and turn it into good research. Funders like Open Philanthropy have often found that they can't deploy as much as they'd like, because the absorptive capacity of the field is limited by senior researchers, mentorship, and good research taste.

So when I imagine a massive scale-up, like 10x or 100x more funding and effort, what has to change is that AI systems themselves become the thing that absorbs the money. You'd need AIs that can act more or less as research engineers, and eventually research scientists. Given a fuzzy goal like "figure out whether this interpretability technique actually tells us something about deception," they'd need to break it into experiments, run them, notice when results look weird, debug their own code, and come back with something a human can evaluate.

Concretely, a few capabilities matter. One is long-horizon reliability: working coherently for days or weeks on a project without drifting or compounding errors. Another is judgment, knowing which of ten possible next steps is worth doing. That's the "research taste" piece, and it's what's scarce among humans too. A third, which people underrate, is the ability to be checked. If you have a thousand AI agents producing research, the bottleneck shifts to verification. You need outputs that are legible and reproducible, and ideally AIs that can critique each other's work in ways humans can spot-check.

Then there's the trust question. To pour huge amounts of compute and money into AI-driven research, especially safety research, you need some confidence that the systems are actually trying to help and aren't sandbagging or subtly steering things. There's a bootstrapping problem: you want to use AI to solve alignment, but you need some alignment to trust the AI doing that work. So I think the realistic path is incremental. Hand off tasks where verification is cheap, build up track records and tooling, and expand the scope of delegation as trust is earned.

My overall take is that the money is almost the easy part. If AI systems hit roughly the level of a competent junior-to-mid researcher who works fast and doesn't get tired, the world could plausibly spend orders of magnitude more on things like safety research, and it would actually turn into progress rather than just piling up in a bank account. The question is whether we'll be ready to use that window well when it arrives, because the same capabilities that make the scale-up possible are also the ones that make the stakes much higher.

r001.rationale: It identifies the limited number of people able to turn grants into good research, including a shortage of senior researchers and mentors, as a bottleneck to scaling funding and effort.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems would need judgment to choose which of several possible next steps is worth pursuing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that right now, if you look at how AI progress actually happens, it's still pretty bottlenecked on humans. You have a relatively small number of researchers and engineers at a handful of labs who are coming up with the ideas, running the experiments, interpreting the results, deciding what to try next. And the compute is scaling fast, but the human labor that directs that compute is not scaling nearly as fast. You can't just hire ten times as many top-tier ML researchers in a year.

So when I think about what a massive scaling of funding and effort would actually require from the AI systems themselves, the key thing is that the systems have to be able to absorb that funding productively. Money and compute are only useful if there's something that can convert them into progress. And at some point, the only way to get the kind of scale-up people are imagining is for the AI systems to take over a large fraction of the work that humans are currently doing in the research process.

Concretely, that means a few things. The systems need to be able to operate autonomously over long time horizons, so not just answer a question or write a function, but take a vague research direction, break it into experiments, run them, notice when something's going wrong, debug it, and iterate for days or weeks without a human babysitting every step. They need to be able to form and update beliefs about what's promising, which is a pretty different skill from pattern-matching on existing solutions. And they need to be reliable enough that you can actually trust the output at scale, because if you have a million AI agents doing research and ten percent of them are quietly producing garbage, that's a disaster, not a speedup.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that this requires the systems to be good at the messy, unglamorous parts. A lot of what makes a human researcher valuable isn't the brilliant insight, it's the taste, the judgment about which of fifty possible experiments is worth running, and the ability to notice when a result is too good to be true. If the AI can do the flashy parts but not that, you haven't really unlocked the scaling, you've just moved the bottleneck.

So I guess my short answer is that the scaling requires AI systems that are something like competent, autonomous, reasonably trustworthy junior-to-mid-level researchers, operating at a scale where you can throw compute at them and get more research out. And once you're there, that's exactly the regime where things could start moving very, very fast, which is also why I think it's the regime we should be most careful about.

r001.rationale: It says AI progress is bottlenecked by a small number of human researchers and engineers, whose labor cannot scale as quickly as compute or funding.

r002.rationale: It describes systems choosing what to try next and judging which experiments are worth running, communicating the need to select research problems.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether AI systems can actually accelerate the research itself. More funding can buy more compute and let you hire more people, but you’d really like AI systems that can take an open-ended research problem, come up with promising experiments, run them, interpret the results, and decide what to try next.

And that requires more than being able to give a good answer to a question. It requires being reliable over a much longer sequence of decisions, recognizing when an approach isn’t working, and not needing a human to constantly steer you back on track. If every additional AI researcher requires a lot of supervision from a human researcher, then human attention becomes the bottleneck.

So I’d be looking for evidence that you can give these systems more resources and get substantially more useful research out, without needing a proportional increase in human oversight. That would make a really large expansion of funding and effort much more compelling.

r001.rationale: It says human attention becomes the bottleneck when each additional AI researcher needs substantial supervision, identifying limited researcher availability as a constraint.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing experiments and deciding what to try next within an open-ended research problem, but does not say the systems would decide which problems to work on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing would be AI systems that can substantially accelerate AI research itself. It’s one thing to have a system that helps you write code or brainstorm an experiment. It’s another to have a system that can take a research question, design experiments, run them, interpret the results, and keep making progress with relatively little human supervision.

If you had that, then spending more on compute could effectively buy you more researchers. And that could justify a really dramatic increase in investment, because you’d be investing in systems that help you build the next generation of systems.

But reliability matters a lot here. You need the systems to do useful work over long stretches, and you need to be able to tell whether they’re actually making progress. So I wouldn’t think of it as a single benchmark threshold. I’d be looking for evidence that these systems can meaningfully shorten the research and development cycle.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could make compute effectively buy more researchers, but it does not identify the availability of people as a bottleneck to scaling funding and effort.

r002.rationale: The response describes working on a given research question, but does not say the systems would decide which problems to work on.
